title: Build a candidate shortlist with evidence, not guesswork
description: Define the hiring bar, calibrate a small sample, and build a sourced shortlist your team can review.
introduction: Candidate sourcing becomes useful when the shortlist explains why each person fits. A longer list is not automatically a better one, especially when profiles are duplicated, evidence is shallow, or the hiring bar was never made explicit.

Strawberry can search approved professional sources, connect profiles with relevant work, and organize the result around the criteria your team actually uses. Begin with a small sample so your judgment shapes the wider search.

sections.title: Define the hiring bar before searching
paragraphs: Separate hard requirements such as location, eligibility, compensation, and must-have experience from softer signals such as seniority, technical depth, startup experience, or communication evidence. Existing scorecards, job descriptions, prior searches, and examples of strong or rejected candidates can sharpen the rubric when they are available.
Use examples to clarify the evidence that matters without turning one person's biography into the requirement. Keep protected or irrelevant personal characteristics out of the search.

sections.title: Calibrate a small sample before scaling
paragraphs: Search a varied first group across the approved sources and review it before expanding. Fewer than ten candidates is often enough to reveal that a criterion is too broad, too narrow, or being interpreted differently than the hiring manager intended.
If nobody in the sample meets the bar, stop and clarify. Scaling a weak search only produces a larger weak list.

skills.context: Use this to define the rubric, calibrate the first sample, and build a sourced shortlist.

sections.title: Research the strongest candidates deeply enough
paragraphs: For a larger pool, collect inexpensive signals first and deepen only the strongest matches. Relevant evidence may come from LinkedIn, GitHub, portfolios, personal sites, talks, posts, or other public professional work.
Cross-reference the ATS or tracker before presenting the shortlist. Check identity, duplicates, prior contact, and current pipeline state, and keep real source links beside every material fit claim.

sections.title: Make the shortlist easy to challenge
paragraphs: Deliver the fields the team needs, an overall assessment, evidence against the important criteria, caveats, confidence, and the number of profiles reviewed and filtered. Include a few candidates set aside and why, especially early in the process, so the team can correct the judgment.

Once the team accepts the rubric, sources, fields, and review method, preserve them as a custom skill. Draft outreach only for an approved shortlist, keep it grounded in verified professional context, and leave messages reviewable until sending is explicitly approved.

skills.context: Use this after shortlist approval to draft relevant candidate outreach.
Use this when the accepted sourcing process should be shared across the hiring team.
